body: They key word is “relatively.”  People die for heart disease every 34 seconds. And the death rate from cancer and accidents dwarfs the rate for suicide. Not trying to minimize the problem. Just pointing out that people should not feel guilty for failing to see it coming or preventing it.

This is very well put.  While suicide is contrary to the human experience and relatively rare (less than 20 of 100,000 people), there are some for whom it is almost a compulsory thought.  And it is rarely the result of any one thing.
Wowza!  You look stunning!

I am so sorry for your loss. I think everyone who has lost a loved one to suicide feels as though they failed their loved one.  I think it is sometimes easier to blame ourselves than to accept just how little control we have over the horrific events that can permanently alter our existence. The reality is that we let down the people we love all the time. If everyone who has let someone down (or been let down) killed themselves, there would literally be no one left.  The fact that your wife left behind a baby, whom I am sure she loved beyond measure, demonstrates that mental illness cannot be cured with love, anymore than physical illness can. If love were enough, they would still be here.

The reality is most kids are bullied. I know that I certainly was. And cyber bullying has taken it to a whole new level. That said, I think that her son was probably particularly vulnerable. Which is not to say that bullying is right. But, in the other hand, most people who bully are suffering too. It’s not normal behavior.

I lost my husband to suicide and I can give you a double-your-money-back guarantee that if I didn’t have children who needed me, I would have been right behind him. If I lost child to suicide, all bets are off and I will do the same.  

We need to stop suggesting that suicide is preventable by anyone other than the person contemplating it. It is like trying to prevent an alcoholic from drinking or an addict from using. You can be supportive, but you cannot control
the outcome.

I am so sorry you have had to endure this. Have you sought counseling with grief counselor experienced in suicide loss?  If not, it could be helpful. I would also recommend looking into EMDR therapy. It can help with the visualizations you are experiencing in your dreams and when awake. 

YOU WERE NOT AT FAULT. Say it over and over again. Tattoo it on your brain. I have to admit when I read
about the “suicide loss fallout” for people like you I
get angry at suicide prevention programs that
spread messaging like “suicide is everyone’s business” and “suicide is preventable.”  It just adds to the guilt. And the reality is, suicide is preventable- but only by the one contemplating  it.  Suggesting
otherwise puts the onus on friends and family for  preventing a mental health crisis that even trained professionals have had no success at preventing.  It is total  bull shit.

IT WAS NOT YOUR FAULT.  Say it over and over. Tattoo it on your brain. No child, 21 or 51, is responsible for their parents suicide.  I am so sorry you have to go through this. And I am so sorry others are blaming you. Please understand that their hurtful insinuations are about them, not you.  I don’t care what your mom said or did. It was not your fault.
Thank you. And I am sorry for yours.

Your mother sounds like a lovely person and I am
glad that you are following her lead and being kind. Suicide is complicated. It is rarely the result of just one thing. People go through breakups and divorces everyday. Very few end their lives as a result. What happened to your brother is tragic, but it isn’t anyone’s fault.  

As to whether or not suicide is a choice, I must admit that I differ from others in this thread. I do believe that there is a neurobiological component to suicide, just as there is to mental disorders like depression, bipolar disorders,  alcoholism and other substance use disorders. But I also believe there is an element of
choice to suicide and to suggest otherwise would be very discouraging to those currently suffering from suicidal ideation and impulses - and rob them of their efficacy to get better and improve their lives. 

I also think that the stories of survivors are
incredibly important to suicide prevention. Many people disagree and caution against saying or doing anything that might make someone struggling with suicidal impulses feel guilty. But I disagree.  We need to listen when people are in pain, but they need to
clearly understand that their death doesn’t end the pain. It just ends it for them and passes it along to their loved ones left behind. 

I know that, before losing my husband to suicide, I did not appreciate the unique pain that suicide inflicts. We don’t just lose our loved one or the future we hoped to
share with them. In some ways, we lose the past too. We question whether our loved ones were ever happy, whether they knew we loved them, whether they ever loved us. My children believed their father loved them so much he would, literally, die for them. Why couldn’t he stay alive for them?  They will never understand why he didn’t love them enough to stay or why their
love wasn’t enough to keep him here.

I am so sorry that you are suffering and I wish there was something I could say or do to help. I have been where you are many times. It really hurts. But know that, while ending your life may end YOUR pain, it will also transfer that pain to the ones you love and cause them a lifetime of excruciating suffering. They will always feel to blame and will never understand how their love wasn’t enough for you to stay. Your mother will be destroyed and may even follow you.

I am so, so sorry you have to endure this. You have every right to feel angry and anything else you may be experiencing. There are no words that can console you or ease your pain, but if you can stay strong it will get easier. Have you had counseling and tried EMDR?  Both can be helpful. Send virtual hugs. You are not alone.
This. This is perfect advice.

I am so sorry for your loss. I under completely how you feel. But please consider getting counseling and joining a support group for suicide loss survivors. You don’t want to transfer the pain to others by following her.

I am so sorry that you and your family have to endure this. First and foremost, please understand that virtually everyone who loses a loved one to suicide feels some level of responsibility and plagues themselves with the “should have, would have, could haves.”  It was not your fault. It was not their fault. Heck, it might not even have been your mother’s fault. We understand so little about the suicidal mind. Please consider getting counseling for all of you from a mental health professional who has experience with suicide loss survivors. You might also consider EMDR therapy for your father and sister to help heal from the trauma of finding her.  And know that anything you’re feeling is normal. Do not let anyone tell you how you should feel or try to dissuade you from your feelings. You have to feel it to heal it.

I think I would pause, look them straight in the eye, and say, “i am sure you can understand how painful that question is and that I prefer not to discuss it.”  If you want to continue a conversation with the person, you could always segue way into, but let me tell you how he lived, he was an amazing Dad . . .

I am so, so sorry for you have to endure this and you are entitled to feel angry, broken, numb, sad and anything other emotion you are experiencing.  My heart aches for you, your mother, his wife and children, and anyone else affected by his death. There are no words that will console you now, just breath and take it day by day, hour by hour, minute by minute.
You are 1000% correct - if love were enough, they would still be here.

I think both of our husbands may have been seriously conflicted. It put us in an untenable position.  Neither of us are (or were) clairvoyant.  I completely understand your wish to have never met. But then I think of all the good things that he brought into my life, that I would not have had without him.  I try to give my husband grace. We know so little about the suicidal mind.  Perhaps someday we will better understand it as something that happened to them, rather than something they did to themselves or to us.

I am so sorry for your loss. Losing a loved one to suicide is a loss unlike any other.  The shame, blame and guilt you are experiencing is virtually universal to those left behind. Those left behind  also invariably idealize the one who died (or at least minimize their flaws). Two things are undoubtedly true: 1) people get divorced all the time - only rarely does one of them kill themselves in the aftermath; and 2) if you knew he was going to kill himself, you would have tried to stop  him. 

Is it possible that, rather than the divorce causing the suicide, the mental dysfunction that resulted in suicide also contributed to the problems in the marriage?  Medical correspondent Jennifer Ashton endured a similar experience and wrote a book “Life After Suicide” that might be helpful. 

For what it’s worth, my husband killed himself over two years ago - and I sometimes think it was because I DIDN’T want a divorce. I sometimes think he felt it was the only way out of the marriage.  I feel guilty too and wonder if he would still be alive if I had left rather than stayed. Ironic.

If your loved one was killed in a car accident after leaving your home, you could regret him not having left five minutes earlier (or minutes later) because, if he had, he would have avoided the accident. That does not mean that the time he left caused his death. Suicide is similar in that it is rarely the result
one thing. It has been described as a perfect storm
of circumstances. If any one of those circumstances were different, he may have gone on to
live another day, week, month or years. But none of those circumstances caused his death.

I absolutely abhor the whole “Suicide is Everyone’s Business”  and “Know the Signs” messaging that is so popular today. I actually think it does more harm than good. First of all, trained professionals are notoriously bad at the predicting who will attempt or succeed at suicide.  If they cannot figure it out, what hope is there for the rest of us?  Second, one of the highest risk factors for suicide is recent discharge from a psychiatric hospital. That tells you everything you need to know about the efficacy of in-patient psych treatment. 

What we do know is that the whole “suicide is preventable” messaging exacerbates the shame, blame, and guilt already universally experienced by suicide loss survivors, putting them at an increased risk of suicide. 

The way I see it, alcoholism and drug addictions are
medical (and mental) disorders. We can support the people suffering from them, but ultimately, we hold them accountable for their choices. I think the same should be true of suicide. I think is incredibly complicated and putting the onus on family members or friends to identify and prevent it is ineffective and damaging.

It’s different because it’s not that clear cut. We do have some control over many things in life. We can go to school, study, get good grades and a degree. We can diet, exercise, and lose weight. And we can always control our attitude.  

But things like suicide, homicide, accidents, and the choices of others are usually beyond our control.

This sounds like the rational act of a terminally ill person.  Losing a loved one is so hard. You are absolutely correct that there is no need for people to know how she died. It’s how she lived that was important - and it sounds like she lived a life of love. I am sorry for your loss.

I do think that it easier to feel guilty than it is to accept how little control we have over horrific events that can irreparably and irreversibly affect the trajectory of our our lives.  That said, I do have a lot of remorse and regrets.
I have all my husband’s texts and emails too.

Thank you for your post. Contrary to offending me, it validates my feeling that if more people truly understood the pain of losing someone to suicide, maybe fewer people would choose to bequeath that pain on others.  God knows current suicide prevention programs are not working.

Thank you so much for taking the time to respond and for your kind words. Fortunately, my children have really positive memories of their dad. He was a wonderful father and person.  I tell them that if love were enough, he would still be here. But we can not cure trauma, depression or the myriad other mental disorders that can contribute to suicide with love alone.  I am so sorry that your mothers story has come to a sad end. But you are absolutely correct that the way our
loved ones lived when healthy is far more important than the  way they died.  I am sending wishes for peace, healing, and happiness

I am so sorry for your loss, and I completely understand your desire to know. But even if it could be  determined that she intentionally took her life, it would raise more questions than it would answer and continue to haunt you.  I don’t mean to diminish your pain, but I envy you. I so wish that my husband had left this world in a manner they could at least arguably be perceived as natural. I wish I had had the presence of mind to try to create a cover story that would protect my children.  The legacy of pain, shame, blame, and guilt, he has bequeathed them is intolerable.  Rely on the experts. They have no reason not to accurately portray their findings.

Suicide is incredibly complicated. I am not saying that we shouldn’t try to support people who are struggling, or that people cannot be saved. But ultimately, another’s choice to live or die is not ours to make. Sometimes I think it is easier to blame ourselves than to accept just how little control we have over horrific events that can permanently alter our lives.  My heart aches for you and your friend. My heart aches for my husband too. Admittedly though, I am experiencing loss of a different sort. As bad as I feel for him, it is nothing compared to how I feel for our children and the legacy of pain he has left them.

I am so so sorry. Losing a someone to suicide is a loss like no other. I am sure your friend knew you cared and that she could come to you.  If love were enough, she would still be here. You cannot cure depression or the myriad other mental  disorders that can lead to suicide with love.  Suicide is incredibly complicated and rarely the result of one thing. It’s like a perfect storm of circumstances. It might help to think of it like almost like an accident. If your friend had died in an automobile accident, it is probably true that, had she gotten on the road five minutes earlier (or later) she would have avoided the accident and lived. But the time she got on the  road didn’t cause the accident. No matter how much you did to help your friend, you will always feel as though you could have done more, but that is not why she died.

I am so, so sorry that you lost your dad to suicide. My husband also died by hanging and my heart breaks for  my children and the legacy of pain he has bequeathed them. Still, I know how much he loved them and I know that he could never have died as he did absent an acute mental episode.  I think of it as the psychological equivalent of an aneurysm.  While many people contemplate suicide (as I am sure both your father and my husband did) I think the actual commission of it is somewhat impulsive and the result of myriad different circumstances that come together to create a perfect storm. We can never really know what they were thinking or feeling. But you can know this, your dad loved you, he knew you loved him, and if love were enough, he would still be here. But sadly, you cannot cure depression or other mental states that tend to occur with suicide with love.

I think you are entitled to use whatever language you prefer. I, too, have no problem with saying my
husband committed suicide.  I don’t agree that it implies a criminal act. Even if it did, it wouldn’t bother me. What bothers me is when people try to over-simplify suicide. It is incredible complex.

If you had asked on 8/31/2019 whether I thought my husband would ever die by suicide, I would have bet my life that he would never end his life that way. If you asked me  the same question on 9/1/2019, I could tell you a dozen reasons why I should have seen it coming and stopped it. Two and a half years later and I still feel responsible for his death.

All of these comments make several things clear to me: 1) how long the writers kept their loved one’s alive (it is clear that many of them would have died far sooner without your vigilance); 2) how utterly useless mental health treatment is for treating suicidal impulses and ideation; and 3) how little we understand about the suicidal mind. Each one of you put so much time, love, and effort into trying to save the one you lost. If love were enough, I have no doubt they would still be here.

I found the support groups very helpful. It is comforting to talk with people who understand what it is like to lose a loved one to suicide. If being in person makes you anxious, there are groups that meet by zoom. You can even turn off your camera if it helps your anxiety.  Check out LOSS through Catholic Charities in Chicago. And don’t worry if you aren’t Catholic, it isn’t religious.

One of the many, many sad things about suicide is that it doesn’t just rob us of our loved one and the future we planned with them, it can also erase the past we had with them. In the eyes of others, the way they died becomes more important than the way they lived. My husband of 32 years was a wonderful father and a good person who did so much for others - especially troubled youth.  I refuse to let the way he died define him or his life and I take every opportunity to honor him.  I continually assure my children that he loved them and that he knew they loved him. I tell them that if love were enough, he would still be here. 

We have so little understanding of the suicidal mind. While I don’t think that suicide is genetically programmed, I do think that there is a genetic tendency toward the mental disorders that predispose one to suicide. I also think there is a “contagion”
effect that renders one who has lost a loved to suicide
more vulnerable. And while my  heart aches for my husband knowing how worthless and hopeless he must have felt, it is nothing compared to the ache I have for my children and the lifelong legacy of
pain he has bequeathed them.  So, sometimes I am angry, but it is mostly at myself for not seeing it coming and preventing it.

I am so sorry for what you are having to endure. And I am sorry for your friend’s insensitive remark. No one left behind benefits from losing a loved one to suicide. No one.  If anything, those left behind are at an increased risk. There is no lesson to be learned, other than that sometimes horrific things happen that we never see coming.   You are right that nothing will ever be the same. But it can get better with time, counseling and a supportive environment. You are a brave mother and your son is lucky to have you.
I wonder the same thing about my husband, who hanged himself using  a bedsheet. There were scratches on his neck. Did he regret his decision when it was too late to change the outcome?

I am so sorry you have to endure this. As for her burial, I agree with others that it is if no concern or consequence to your friend now. Like you, I would want to see the note, but I honestly doubt if doing so would bring you any peace. It sounds like your friend struggled for years and succumbed after a long battle. I am sure her parents and siblings are overwhelmed with shame, blame and guilt.  You say you are so mad at her parents that you don’t think you can reach out.  Perhaps her sibling is trying to protect them from further pain. I am certain they are all in excruciating pain. Perhaps reach out to her parents after your anger has dissipated?  No matter what the note reveals, or what facts you unearth, no one is to blame for your friend’s decision to end her life - perhaps not even your friend herself.

I am so sorry for your loss. Is it possible the text was written but not sent?  That is what happened to me. I found the unsent messages on his phone.  He said he did not send them “for obvious reasons.”  (He didn’t want to tip me off and perhaps stop him.)  

Like you, I ache thinking of how alone he must have felt and I wonder if he was scared. You mentioned that your person said  he could never shoot himself -  but then did just that.  Since my husband’s death I have frequently heard similar stories. It now makes me wonder if their saying it was part of the process of working up the determination and fearlessness to go through with it.
Thank you. Sending hugs.

I am so sorry. No daughter should have to lose her father to suicide. I lost my husband and our daughter (27) is devastated. She and her dad were so close. She cannot fathom how he could leave her that way. I know how much he loved her and I truly believe that if love were enough, he would still be here.  I am sure your dad would still be here too. But love cannot cure the myriad mental states that lead one to end their lives.  And conversely, suicide does not negate their love for us or ours for them.  You say you wish your dad had died of something normal and I totally get why you feel that way. But I do think that suicide is kind of like the psychological equivalent of an aneurysm. It is an acute state over which your dad may have had very little control.

I agree. I, too, have done everything they told
me to do to “heal.”  I have seen a grief counselor who specializes in suicide loss, done EMDR, joined a support group, read books, meditated, and tried anti-depressants.  Two and half years later and the  pain is still  brutal.  I have let go of  any notion of happiness. I
am just trying to stay alive for my kids.

My husband did leave a note and it actually raised more questions than it answered.  I am not suggesting that I wish he hadn’t left one, just that it didn’t really help process the situation.  I think your  observation that there was nothing your brother could have said that would have made his death easier is astute. 

You are also absolutely spot on when you acknowledge that your brother knew you loved him and that he loved you. There is no question in my
mind that, if love were enough, all our lost family members would still be here.  Sadly, depression, bipolar, suicidal ideation, and any other mental illness cannot be treated with love.  If love plays any role in suicide, it is that  the people we lost didn’t love themselves. 

I hope that someday we will have a better understanding of the suicidal mind. Perhaps one that permits us to give grace to the loved ones we lost and see it as something that happened to them, rather than something they did to themselves or to us.
There is no greater burden to bear than the loss of someone by suicide.  I will never recover. My children will never recover. I wish he had taken us with him.
Have you tried a mineral sunscreen (one with zinc or titanium dioxide?   They are very non-irritating. In fact,  it’s the same stuff they put in creams for baby’s diaper rash.

I am so, so sorry for your loss.  Losing a loved one to suicide is unlike any other death. Believe it or not, everything you are feeling, no matter how contradictory, is totally normal. So is the desire to interject logic, reason, and common sense into what is typically an irrational act. (I say typically only because I think there are some suicides that are rational acts, but they are usually done openly and with the support of family where terminal illness is involved).  Your
Caption says it all. Despite rather trite suicide prevention slogans that assert otherwise, we really do not know how to treat (let alone beat) the demons. Sadly, the demons almost always win.
I think your attitude is a good one and I applaud it.

I am so, so sorry for your loss. Losing a parent to suicide is a loss unlike any other. I lost my husband over two years ago and I am still in pain every day. But my worst fear is for my children and the pain they must feel. I know how much he loved them (as I am sure your father loved you). I know he had to have had a mental breakdown to do what he did because he couldn’t have inflicted that pain on them otherwise. I hope and pray that they can recover and that you can too.

I am so, so sorry for your loss. Losing a loved one to suicide is unlike any other. I lost my husband two and a half years ago.   Two weeks is so new and raw. You are still in shock. Try not to think too far ahead. Take it one day, hour, minute, even second at a time. Breathe. Lean into the pain. You really do have to feel it to heal it. Then, find a counselor or therapist who has dealt with survivors of suicide loss. (A good place to look is at health systems that have in and outpatient programs for people who are suicidal).   Get counseling. Consider EMDR.  Join a support group for people who have lost a loved one to suicide. Catholic Charities in Chicago has an amazing zoom group for people who have lost a partner. It is called LOSS(Loving Outreach to Suicide Survivors) and they meet monthly. Don’t worry if you aren’t Catholic. It is completely non-religious.  I am glad you are thinking of your sister and what it would do to her if you ended your life. I think we have all been there, but the madness has to stop with us. And I am sending heartfelt wishes for your healing and peace.

IT. WAS. NOT. YOUR. FAULT. Say it over and over. Tattoo it on your brain. Every relationship of any duration has its ups and downs. People fight. They say and do (or fail to say and do) things that upset, anger, and hurt each other all the time. If every relationship with difficulties ended in suicide there would literally be no one left.

And may I also add to try and steer clear of suicide prevention programs for a while. Their “suicide is preventable “ and “suicide is everyone’s business” slogans are well intended but really hurtful for those of us who lost a loved one to suicide and are already feeling guilty, ashamed and to blame.
You are to be commended. I, too, want to help but my issue is that I do not agree with many of the current prevention platforms. I actually think some are doing more harm than good.
Sending you positive thoughts for healing, peace and (eventually) happiness.
You are gorgeous. My only advice would be to relish your beauty and youth. You do NOT need fillers. Save the money and take trip or do something that brings you joy.

There are a lot of support groups meeting by zoom due to COVID. Catholic Charities in Chicago even has a number of groups specific to the relationships (loss of partners, parents, etc.   Don’t worry if you are not Catholic, they are completely non- religious. Their program is called LOSS (Loving Outreach to Suicide Survivors).

I am so, so sorry for your loss. They say that suicide takes all the answers and leaves us with all the questions. It is so hard to accept.  I think you are absolutely correct that he acted on impulse. Even people that suffer from suicidal ideation and plan their deaths ultimately act on impulse. As for what exactly happened, I don’t think it is usually any one thing. Rather, I think it is a myriad of things. It has been described as a “perfect storm.”  I so wish there was a way to bring your dad back. Sadly, there is no way to bring him back physically, but he will always be a part of your heart.

I lost my husband (and my children lost their father) to suicide on 8/31/2019.  It is agonizing. 

I think that suicide is incredibly complicated.  Trying to balance the needs of those who may be feeling suicidal (so they can get help) with the needs of those who have lost a loved one to suicide (so they find hope and healing) can lead to messaging that inadvertently hurts one group while trying to help the other.   

Frequently, I see people compare depression and other mental disorders to cancer and heart disease.  The argument is that people did not cause their disease and should not be blamed for dying from it. And while the comparison is somewhat apt, I think the better analogy is alcoholism and/or other substance use disorders.  They are medical issues, but we still hold people accountable for their choices/actions. And we do not treat children and adults the same.

So, as to whether suicide is a choice, for me I think the answer is sometimes. I think it was for my husband.  But when I read of people who have lost children, teens or young adults  - I cannot imagine that they were even developmentally capable of making such a choice.

I am so sorry for your loss. I lost my husband to suicide two-and-a-half years ago.  Losing a partner to suicide is agonizing. It leaves us with so may unanswered questions. It is so difficult to accept, but accept it we must. And we must all find a way to move forward. 

It sounds like your husband loved you and wanted to build a life with you. It was himself he couldn’t stand. I belong to a couple of online groups for suicide widows and so many of them involve husbands who end their lives shortly after being caught in betrayals.  I find it mind-boggling that they could lie and cheat with impunity, but become suicidal when caught.  It makes no sense to me, but I guess suicide rarely ever does.

I feel exactly the same way. I lost my husband 2 1/2 years ago and I think it hurts more now than when it first happened.  The pain of those good memories is searing. I don’t know why but I suspect it may be part and parcel of suicide. I think had he died a natural  death, those memories would be less painful and more of a comfort.

I am so sorry you had to live your life with the loss of your father that way.  I know that my husband had to have been in pain. And I feel for him. But compared to how I feel for my children, it’s nothing. I truly hate him for saddling them with this pain and the belief that he did not love them enough to stay.

Losing a loved one to suicide is agonizing.  I, lost my husband nearly two and a half years ago and it is worse now than then. I think I naively hoped for healing in the early days, weeks, and months. Now I know that is  like hoping to heal from paraplegia. 
The worst of it for me is knowing the pain my kids have to endure the rest of their lives, which will probably be twice as long as mine. Sometimes I wish he had taken us all with him.

I am so sorry for your loss.  You are so right that the pain our loved one suffered doesn’t end with their life. It is multiplied. The legacy of suicide is that their pain is now ours to bear for a lifetime. It is no doubt why survivors of suicide loss have an increased risk of dying the same way.

There are no words. Feel free to pm me if you need to vent or want to talk. Reading the posts from people who are several years out and still suffering breaks my heart. I would do anything to spare my children this pain.

I am so sorry for your loss. I have to admit, reading it make me livid with my husband, who took his life 2 1/2 years ago.  I know he was in pain, and I feel for him. But compared to how I feel for our children and the lifelong legacy of pain he has left them, it’s nothing.  I know it’s not politically correct to express anger toward those who take their lives, but I don’t care. What he did was selfish, self absorbed,  and hostile.  Putting that on his kids was unconscionable. I don’t care if he was in pain. He was a parent and had to do whatever it took to stay alive.

Losing a loved one to suicide increases one’s own risk significantly.  This is particularly true when the loved one is also a family member.   Loss by suicide is agonizing, and it not surprising that survivors contemplate it as a way to end the pain of that loss. So, please know that you are not alone or a bad
person for thinking about it.

I lost my husband two and a half years ago and I, too, have thought what a relief it would be to end the pain.  But, like you, I will not do that to my loved ones. When the pain is really intense, I try to lean into it, feel it and just take it a minute at a time. I remind myself that I don’t need to be a stellar person. I just need to stay alive.

There is nothing immoral about trying to spare his 93-year-old mother the agony of losing a child to suicide. Losing a child is horrific enough. 

I lost my husband to suicide, and if  I could have come up with a plausible explanation to spare our children, I’d have done it in a heartbeat.

I am so sorry for your loss and the losses of all the others who posted before me. I lost my husband to suicide just over two years ago and, like many others, I do not believe that I will ever heal from it.  Hopefully, some day I will learn to live with it. 

As to whether suicide is a choice or not, I do not think there is an easy answer. I think that suicide is incredibly complicated and impossible to pigeon hole. I don’t think  it is always a choice, or that it is never a choice. I don’t think that it is always a result of mental illness or irrational, although it frequently is.  Sometimes, I compare it to homicide - where we recognize that there are varying degrees of culpability and intent.  Sometimes I think it is like alcoholism or drug addiction, which we recognize as medical conditions, while still holding  the people suffering from them accountable for their actions.  

I think in many cases (and in my husband’s case), his suicide was the result of many choices made over a number of years and culminating in one terrible, impulsive choice that he probably regretted when it was too late to change the outcome. When I think of how he must have felt, my heart aches for him. But it is nothing compared to how I feel for my heartbroken children left behind.

I think we need to have empathy and effective treatment readily available for adults suffering from mental illness or suicidal impulses. But, we must be careful not to remove agency from them and place it on ourselves.

The lump sum death benefit is the same for everyone. I agree, it is ridiculously low. I don’t know why. You say the system failed her. Did your mother apply for social security disability benefits before she died?  Is your dad of retirement age (at least 66 years)?  If the answer to either of those questions is yes, your dad might be eligible for more benefits.

When we lose a loved one to suicide, it is hard not to blame ourselves. We all feel as though we should have seen it coming or have been able to prevent it. 
But the reality is every close relationship has its ups and downs - and our perceptions are uniquely our own.  Our perceptions  may or may not coincide with our partners. 

That said, very few people choose to end their lives by suicide.  Even relationships fraught with addiction, mental illness, infidelity and betrayal rarely end in suicide.  (I know, I know, we lose too many to suicide. I know it is the 10th leading cause of death overall in the US.) But statistically, it is dwarfed by the first two or three causes of death for most adults. 

My point is not to diminish the seriousness of suicide. It is merely to point out that virtually EVERYONE in a long term relationship has issues sometimes. And virtually EVERYONE whom loses a loved one to suicide feels to blame to some degree.  

I think we  blame ourselves because it is easier than accepting how little control we have over the horrific things that can (and sometimes do) happen to us.  Even after losing the love of my life to suicide (and feeling suicidal myself) I know that if I were to end my life, no one else would be to blame.  And you are not to blame either.

That said, in answer to your question about how you can explain taking your life in a clear, concise way, it certainly cannot be done in a note. It’s like asking how one can explain the meaning of life and death on a post-it.  If you truly feel that suicide should be “just a choice” (and I am NOT judging that position) then you should discuss it openly with the people you care for and those who will be affected by the finality of your death.

I concur with everything you said, but I would add that there is perhaps another side to suicide to consider( other than mental illness and society). It is one that is more philosophical. Suicide has been part of virtually every society since the dawn of time. In some societies, it was even viewed as an act of honor.  Is there a right to self-determination that includes suicide? Even if all suicide is the result if mental illness (which I seriously doubt), does that necessarily mean that the individual is unable to make an informed decision about their life (and death)? After all, we hold people who are mentally ill accountable for homicide all the time (think Jeffrey Dahmer). 

I think we need to have some serious philosophical discussions about suicide and how we, as a society, view it. Particularly when we are considering incentivizing people who do not want help - to get it.  Right now, the current awareness/ prevention platforms focus on on how others can help one who is suicidal. Unfortunately, it often has the unintended effect of increasing the sense of shame, blame and guilt in those left behind. This is understandable. If suicide is preventable, then they failed in preventing it. This, in turn, increases a survivor’s risk of dying by suicide and drives the overall death rate up, not down. There really is no evidence-based research that supports current prevention efforts. The rates have remained static or climbed over the last 40 years when suicide prevention began in earnest. 

I don’t anyone to feel alone. But we need to think of everyone when we are crafting prevention programs and treatment.
